assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly defines the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) at lag k, and distinguishes it from the ACF at lag k?
options: PACF at lag k is the correlation between X_t and X_(t-k) after removing the linear effect of the intermediate lags X_(t-1) through X_(t-k+1); ACF at lag k makes no such adjustment and reflects both direct and indirect (transmitted-through-shorter-lags) correlation.
PACF only exists for MA processes, and ACF only exists for AR processes.
PACF and ACF are two equivalent formulas for the exact same quantity, differing only in numerical precision.
PACF at lag k is the ACF at lag k divided by the sample size n, used to correct for a small-sample bias.
assessments.explanation: PACF is the correlation at lag k with the effect of all shorter lags partialed out, which is why it isolates a lag's own contribution and gives a sharp cutoff for AR processes where the ACF alone shows gradual, never-quite-zero decay. The “PACF and ACF are two equivalent formulas…” option denies a real distinction between the two functions. The “PACF at lag k is the ACF…” option invents a sample-size correction that isn't what PACF computes. The “PACF only exists for MA processes…” option is false -- both ACF and PACF are defined, and routinely computed, for any stationary series, AR, MA, or mixed.

assessments.prompt: A series' PACF spikes sharply at lag 1 and lag 2, then is statistically indistinguishable from zero at every lag beyond that; its ACF decays gradually across many lags with no clean cutoff. Which model order does this classical signature suggest trying first?
options: This pattern is impossible to see in real data and indicates a bug in the ACF/PACF computation.
ARMA(0,0) -- pure white noise, since a cutoff in either function implies no real structure exists, so the lags shown in the plot should be treated as noise from the sample.
MA(2), because the ACF's gradual decay is the defining signature of a pure MA process.
AR(2), because a PACF that cuts off sharply after lag p (here, p=2) while the ACF decays gradually is exactly the theoretical signature of a pure AR(p) process.
assessments.explanation: A PACF that cuts off sharply after a specific lag with an ACF that decays gradually is the textbook signature of a pure AR(p) process, with p read from the PACF cutoff (here, 2). The “MA(2), because the ACF's gradual decay…” option has the AR/MA signatures backwards; gradual ACF decay paired with a PACF cutoff points to AR, not MA. The “ARMA(0,0) -- pure white noise, since…” option is wrong because a cutoff in PACF at a nonzero lag indicates real structure (an AR component), not the absence of any. The “This pattern is impossible to see…” option is false; this is the routine signature that AR(2) simulations demonstrate.

assessments.prompt: Why do practitioners typically treat ACF/PACF plots as a starting point for candidate ARIMA orders rather than a final answer?
options: Because ACF and PACF can only be computed for series shorter than 100 observations, making them unreliable for most real datasets.
Because sample ACF/PACF values are noisy estimates with confidence bands.
Because plotting libraries round all displayed values to zero decimal places, making the plots too imprecise to read.
Because ACF and PACF plots are only valid for non-stationary series, and become meaningless once a series has been properly differenced.
assessments.explanation: Sample ACF/PACF estimates carry sampling noise, come with confidence bands that make small bars indistinguishable from zero, and real processes are rarely pure AR or pure MA, so the standard workflow uses the plots to propose a short list of candidate orders, then compares actual fits with AIC/BIC and checks residuals for leftover autocorrelation before settling on a final model. The “Because ACF and PACF can only…” option invents a length restriction that doesn't exist. The “Because ACF and PACF plots are only…” option is false; ACF/PACF are computed on stationary (often already-differenced) series specifically to select AR/MA orders. The “Because plotting libraries round all displayed values…” option invents a plotting-precision issue that isn't the actual reason.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague what distinguishes the ACF from the PACF conceptually, why a pure AR(p) process and a pure MA(q) process show opposite cutoff-versus-decay signatures in the two functions, and why a practitioner shouldn't stop at reading the plots alone when choosing an ARIMA order.
assessments.modelAnswer: The ACF at lag k is the raw correlation between a series and a copy of itself shifted back k steps, whether that correlation is direct or transmitted indirectly through the shorter lags in between. The PACF at lag k asks a more specific question: once you've already accounted for the linear effect of every shorter lag (1 through k-1), how much additional correlation is left at lag k? That conditioning lets PACF isolate a lag's direct contribution rather than mixing it with everything transmitted through nearer lags. This is why a pure AR(p) process and a pure MA(q) process show opposite signatures: an AR(p) process's entire dependence on the past runs through its p most recent lags, so once you control for those p lags in a regression, no longer lag adds anything: the PACF cuts off right after lag p, even though the ACF keeps showing decaying but nonzero correlation at every lag, because those longer-lag relationships are present, just transmitted rather than direct. An MA(q) process is the mirror image: its observed values share no common shock terms once you're more than q steps apart, so its ACF cuts off cleanly after lag q, but expressing that same structure as a regression on past observed values takes an ever-growing autoregression to approximate, which is why its PACF decays gradually instead of cutting off. In practice, though, real series are rarely purely one or the other, and the sample versions of these functions are noisy estimates with confidence bands, so a practitioner uses the plots only to shortlist a couple of plausible (p, q) candidates, then actually fits those candidates and compares them with a penalized criterion like AIC or BIC, and checks the winning model's residuals for any leftover autocorrelation, before trusting a final chosen order.

concepts.title: Unit Root Tests: Augmented Dickey-Fuller and KPSS
concepts.description: A unit root in a series' characteristic equation is the formal condition that produces non-stationarity. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test (null: a unit root is present) and the KPSS test (null: the series is stationary, the opposite convention) are the two standard, complementary hypothesis tests practitioners run together to decide whether a series needs differencing before modeling.
learningObjectives: Explain what a unit root is in the characteristic equation of an autoregressive process and why its presence implies non-stationarity.
State the null and alternative hypotheses of the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test and interpret its p-value correctly.
State the null and alternative hypotheses of the KPSS test and explain how they are the logical opposite of the ADF test's hypotheses.
Run both ADF and KPSS on a series using statsmodels and reconcile agreeing or conflicting results using the standard four-way decision table.
Explain how the outcome of a unit root test formally answers the practical question of whether, and how much, to difference a series before modeling it.

sections.heading: What a Unit Root Is, and Why It Means Non-Stationarity
sections.body:
Go back to the AR(1) equation from earlier in this module, `X_t = phi * X_(t-1) + eps_t`, and rewrite it in terms of its **characteristic equation**: `1 - phi*z = 0`, which has a single root at `z = 1/phi`. The stability condition `|phi| < 1` from the AR/MA/ARIMA concept is exactly equivalent to saying this root lies strictly outside the unit circle (`|z| > 1`). A **unit root** is the boundary case: a root sitting exactly *on* the unit circle, `|z| = 1`, which for AR(1) means `phi = 1` exactly. Then the equation becomes `X_t = X_(t-1) + eps_t`, the random walk used as the non-stationary example throughout this module.

Here is *why* a unit root breaks stationarity. With `phi = 1`, recursive substitution gives `X_t = X_0 + eps_1 + eps_2 + ... + eps_t`: every shock the process has experienced is carried forward with a permanent weight of 1, never decaying. Its variance is `Var(X_t) = t * sigma^2` (for a fixed starting value `X_0`), which grows without bound instead of settling at a constant, violating weak stationarity's constant-variance requirement. With `|phi| < 1`, each shock's weight decays geometrically and the variance converges to a constant, `sigma^2 / (1 - phi^2)`, as `t` grows. For a general AR(p) process, the same idea generalizes: stationarity requires every root of the characteristic polynomial `1 - phi_1*z - phi_2*z^2 - ... - phi_p*z^p = 0` to lie strictly outside the unit circle; a root exactly on it means the process is **integrated** (non-stationary, but stationary after differencing), which is what the "I" in ARIMA is there to fix. This ties the concept back to how `d` gets chosen.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_paths, n = 2000, 500
eps = rng.normal(size=(n_paths, n))

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps, axis=1)                  # phi = 1 exactly: a unit root

stationary_ar1 = np.zeros((n_paths, n))               # phi = 0.8: no unit root
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[:, t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[:, t - 1] + eps[:, t]

# variance ACROSS the 2000 independent paths, at t = 100 and at t = 400
for name, paths in [("random walk", random_walk), ("stationary AR(1)", stationary_ar1)]:
    print(name, "variance at t=100 vs t=400:",
          round(paths[:, 99].var(), 1), "vs", round(paths[:, 399].var(), 1))
# random walk: 99.9 vs 400.4    stationary AR(1): 2.8 vs 2.8
```

The variance is measured across many independent paths at a fixed time, which is what `Var(X_t)` means. The random walk's variance at t=400 is about four times its variance at t=100 (400.4 against 99.9), confirming `Var(X_t) = t * sigma^2`. The stationary AR(1) process has the same variance at both times, near the theoretical `sigma^2 / (1 - 0.8^2)` = 2.78. (Splitting a single path into halves and comparing within-half variances does not show this cleanly, since one random walk path is a single noisy draw.) This growth is the checkable fingerprint a unit root leaves, and the formal tests below detect it statistically from a single series.

sections.heading: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test: Null = Non-Stationary
sections.body:
The **Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test** formalizes the unit-root check into a hypothesis test. Its null and alternative hypotheses are: **H0: the series has a unit root (it is non-stationary)**; **H1: the series is stationary** (or stationary around a deterministic trend, depending on the test's exact specification). Mechanically, ADF regresses the first difference `delta X_t = X_t - X_(t-1)` on `X_(t-1)`, a constant (and optionally a trend term), and enough lagged difference terms `delta X_(t-1), delta X_(t-2), ...` to soak up any leftover autocorrelation in the residuals -- the extra lagged difference terms are the "Augmented" in the name, distinguishing it from the simpler Dickey-Fuller test it generalizes. The test statistic is the t-statistic on the `X_(t-1)` coefficient, but it does **not** follow a standard t-distribution. Under the unit-root null it follows a non-standard distribution (the Dickey-Fuller distribution), so p-values come from the test's own tables, as `adfuller` reports them (it interpolates MacKinnon's response-surface values), not from a t-table. With a constant included (the default `regression="c"`), the 5% critical value of the statistic is about -2.86; more negative statistics reject.

The **interpretation rule** that matters in practice: a **small p-value** (conventionally below 0.05) lets you **reject H0**, giving evidence that the series **is stationary**. A **large p-value** means you **fail to reject H0**, i.e. you don't have sufficient evidence to rule out a unit root, so you'd typically proceed as if the series is non-stationary (with a caveat about what "fail to reject" does and doesn't prove, covered in the misconceptions).

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 500
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

rw_stat, rw_pvalue, *_ = adfuller(random_walk)
ar_stat, ar_pvalue, *_ = adfuller(stationary_ar1)

print(f"random walk:       ADF stat={rw_stat:.3f}, p-value={rw_pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"stationary AR(1):  ADF stat={ar_stat:.3f}, p-value={ar_pvalue:.3f}")
```

The random walk's p-value should come back large (for this seed a hand-written version of the regression gives a statistic near -1.8, well above the -2.86 critical value, so a p-value near 0.4), meaning ADF fails to reject the unit-root null, consistent with non-stationarity. The stationary AR(1) series should give a small p-value (the hand-written statistic is about -6.5, far below the critical value), so ADF rejects the unit-root null and supports stationarity. Both match what is known by construction, which is the point of testing on data with a known answer before trusting the test where you don't know it. (statsmodels is not installed in the environment used to check this lesson; the statistics quoted come from an equivalent hand-written regression, and the exact p-values are unverified.)

sections.heading: The KPSS Test: Null = Stationary (The Opposite Convention)
sections.body:
The **KPSS test** (Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin) is built around the **opposite null hypothesis** from ADF: **H0: the series is (trend-)stationary**; **H1: the series has a unit root**. KPSS works quite differently from ADF. It regresses the series on a constant (and optionally a deterministic trend), accumulates the partial sums of the residuals, and builds a Lagrange-multiplier-type statistic from how much those partial sums drift. The statistic grows large when the residuals don't behave like stationary noise around the fitted level or trend.

The **interpretation rule for KPSS is the mirror image of ADF's**, because the null hypothesis is reversed: a **small p-value** (below 0.05) lets you **reject H0**, giving evidence the series **has a unit root (is non-stationary)**. A **large p-value** means you **fail to reject H0**, consistent with the series being stationary. This reversal is the most common point of confusion in applied unit-root testing: a low p-value means "stationary" under ADF but "non-stationary" under KPSS, and reading one test's p-value with the other's rule gives a flatly backwards conclusion. Note also that statsmodels' `kpss` interpolates p-values from a table, so they are capped between 0.01 and 0.10 and it issues an `InterpolationWarning` when the statistic falls outside the table; a printed 0.100 means "0.10 or larger".

```python
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import kpss

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 500
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.8 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

rw_stat, rw_pvalue, *_ = kpss(random_walk, regression="c")
ar_stat, ar_pvalue, *_ = kpss(stationary_ar1, regression="c")

print(f"random walk:       KPSS stat={rw_stat:.3f}, p-value={rw_pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"stationary AR(1):  KPSS stat={ar_stat:.3f}, p-value={ar_pvalue:.3f}")
```

The random walk's KPSS p-value should be small (the hand-written statistic is about 2.2, far above the 5% critical value of 0.463), rejecting the stationarity null. For the stationary AR(1) series the outcome is less clean: with phi = 0.8 the hand-written statistic is about 0.79, which is above 0.463, so KPSS would reject stationarity for this particular series. This is a known weakness: KPSS over-rejects when a stationary series is highly persistent, because the long-run variance estimate is hard to get right. A less persistent series (phi = 0.75 with another seed, in the first example below, gives a statistic near 0.24) is not rejected. The direction of each conclusion relative to the p-value is opposite to ADF's, which is the reversed-null relationship this section exists to show. (These values come from a hand-written computation, since statsmodels was not available; treat the exact p-values as unverified.)

sections.heading: Running Both Together: The Decision Table Practitioners Actually Use
sections.body:
Because ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses and different power characteristics, practitioners often run **both** and reconcile the results with a four-way decision table (the same four cases appear in the statsmodels documentation):

- **ADF rejects H0 (says stationary) AND KPSS fails to reject H0 (says stationary):** both tests agree: treat the series as stationary with reasonable confidence.
- **ADF fails to reject H0 (says non-stationary) AND KPSS rejects H0 (says non-stationary):** both tests agree: treat the series as non-stationary and difference it (increase `d`) before modeling.
- **ADF rejects H0 (says stationary) AND KPSS rejects H0 (says non-stationary):** the tests conflict. This combination points to a **difference-stationary** series: ADF's evidence of stationarity and KPSS's evidence of a unit root together suggest that differencing is needed. Check the differenced series with both tests again.
- **ADF fails to reject H0 (says non-stationary) AND KPSS fails to reject H0 (says stationary):** the tests conflict in the other direction. This combination suggests a **trend-stationary** series: stationary around a deterministic trend, so the trend should be removed (detrend) and the residuals tested again. It can also reflect low power on a short or noisy sample, in which case more data, a plot, or residual diagnostics after a tentative fit serve as the tiebreaker.

The table answers the question this module keeps returning to: **should I difference this series before modeling it?** Running ADF and KPSS together replaces a guess from a plot with a decision backed by two tests whose error rates are known under their assumptions, and the outcome feeds the differencing order `d` in ARIMA(p, d, q). The `regression` argument matters: with a deterministic trend in the data, use `regression="ct"` in both tests (the default `regression="c"` tests stationarity around a constant, so a trending series looks non-stationary to both).

```python
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

def recommend_differencing(series, alpha=0.05, regression="c"):
    adf_pvalue = adfuller(series, regression=regression)[1]
    kpss_pvalue = kpss(series, regression=regression)[1]

    adf_says_stationary = adf_pvalue < alpha
    kpss_says_stationary = kpss_pvalue >= alpha

    if adf_says_stationary and kpss_says_stationary:
        return "stationary -- no differencing needed", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    if not adf_says_stationary and not kpss_says_stationary:
        return "non-stationary -- difference the series (increase d)", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    if adf_says_stationary and not kpss_says_stationary:
        return "conflicting -- likely difference-stationary, consider differencing", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue
    return "conflicting -- likely trend-stationary (consider detrending) or low test power", adf_pvalue, kpss_pvalue

# recommend_differencing(some_series) -> a plain-language recommendation plus both p-values
```

This function encodes the four-way table above. Even when the tests agree it gives a recommendation, not a certainty, because both tests have false-positive and false-negative rates. The next concept (Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models) moves to a different kind of stochastic process; this differencing decision is the last piece of the stationarity-to-ARIMA pipeline built in this module.

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

rng = np.random.default_rng(20)
n = 400
eps = rng.normal(size=n)

random_walk = np.cumsum(eps)
stationary_ar1 = np.zeros(n)
for t in range(1, n):
    stationary_ar1[t] = 0.75 * stationary_ar1[t - 1] + eps[t]

for name, series in [("random walk", random_walk), ("stationary AR(1)", stationary_ar1)]:
    stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(series)
    verdict = "reject H0 -> evidence of stationarity" if pvalue < 0.05 else "fail to reject H0 -> consistent with a unit root"

The stationary AR(1) series should report a small p-value ('reject H0'), providing evidence of stationarity (hand-written statistic near -7.6). Both outcomes match what is known by construction, which is why testing on synthetic data with a known answer first is good practice. examples.title: A Combined ADF + KPSS Differencing Recommendation Function
examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

def recommend_differencing(series, alpha=0.05, regression="c"):
    adf_p = adfuller(series, regression=regression)[1]
    kpss_p = kpss(series, regression=regression)[1]
    adf_stationary = adf_p < alpha
    kpss_stationary = kpss_p >= alpha

    if adf_stationary and kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "stationary -- no differencing needed"
    elif not adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "non-stationary -- difference the series"
    elif adf_stationary and not kpss_stationary:
        verdict = "conflicting -- likely difference-stationary, consider differencing"
    else:
        verdict = "conflicting -- likely trend-stationary (detrend) or low power"
    return verdict, adf_p, kpss_p

rng = np.random.default_rng(30)
t = np.arange(300)
trend_stationary = 0.05 * t + rng.normal(scale=1.0, size=300)   # stationary AROUND a trend

print(recommend_differencing(trend_stationary, regression="c"))    # trend ignored by both tests
print(recommend_differencing(trend_stationary, regression="ct"))   # trend allowed for in both tests
examples.explanation: The series is noise around a fixed deterministic trend line (0.05 per step), not a trend built up by a random walk. With `regression="c"` both tests test against a constant level, so both see a series whose level is clearly not constant: ADF fails to reject its unit-root null (a hand-written version gives a statistic near 0.1) and KPSS rejects its stationarity null (statistic near 1.9). The table then says 'non-stationary, difference it', which would over-difference a series that is stationary around its trend. With `regression="ct"` both tests allow for the trend and agree the series is stationary (ADF statistic far below the critical value of about -3.4, KPSS statistic near 0.04 against 0.146). The lesson is that the test specification must match the trend structure: pick `"ct"` when a deterministic trend is plausible, and look at a plot. (statsmodels was not run; values come from a hand-written computation and are unverified.)

misconceptions.description: ADF and KPSS test the same null hypothesis, so a low p-value means the same thing for both, and you only really need to run one of them.
misconceptions.clarification: The two tests have opposite null hypotheses: ADF's null is 'a unit root is present (non-stationary)', so a low p-value there means rejecting non-stationarity, i.e. evidence of stationarity. KPSS's null is 'the series is stationary', so a low p-value there means rejecting stationarity, i.e. evidence of a unit root (the opposite conclusion from the same-looking low p-value). Practitioners run both because they can disagree, and the disagreement is diagnostic (it points to a trend-stationary or difference-stationary series), which running only one test would never reveal.

misconceptions.description: A large ADF p-value (failing to reject the unit-root null) definitively proves the series is non-stationary.
misconceptions.clarification: Failing to reject a null hypothesis is not proof that it is true. It means the data did not provide strong enough evidence against it, which happens either because the series really is non-stationary or because the test has low power on that sample (a short series, structural breaks, or a phi close to but inside the stability boundary are classic causes). Treating 'fail to reject' as certainty is the same error as treating any retained null as proven, and it is why practitioners cross-check with KPSS, inspect the series, and consider sample size and structural stability rather than trusting one p-value.

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

def needs_differencing(series, alpha=0.05):
    stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(series)
    # FIXED: a small p-value rejects the unit-root null -> evidence of stationarity -> no differencing needed
    if pvalue < alpha:
        return False   # evidence of stationarity
    return True   # failed to reject unit-root null -> treat as needing differencing

The fix flips the boolean logic: a small p-value (reject H0) means stationary, so differencing is not needed; a large p-value (fail to reject H0) means the unit root can't be ruled out, so differencing is the safer default. This is a common bug because 'small p-value = something significant' is true in general, but what the significance supports depends on which hypothesis is the null. assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague why ADF and KPSS have opposite null hypotheses, how to correctly read a p-value from each, and why running both together -- and reconciling any disagreement -- is the standard formal way to decide whether a series needs differencing before modeling.
assessments.modelAnswer: A unit root exists when a root of a series' characteristic equation lands exactly on the boundary of the AR stability condition, and its presence is what makes a process non-stationary -- shocks never decay, and variance grows without bound over time rather than settling at a fixed value. ADF and KPSS are the two standard hypothesis tests for detecting this, and they have opposite null hypotheses: ADF's null is that a unit root is present (the series is non-stationary), so a small p-value lets you reject that null and concludes the series is likely stationary, while a large p-value means you cannot rule out a unit root. KPSS flips this around entirely -- its null is that the series is stationary, so a small p-value there lets you reject stationarity and concludes the series likely has a unit root, while a large p-value is consistent with stationarity. A small p-value therefore means opposite things depending on which test produced it, the most common point of confusion with these tests, and reading it backwards flips the conclusion. Because the two tests have different statistical power against different kinds of departures from stationarity, and because their nulls are logical opposites, practitioners run both together and reconcile the results with a four-way table: both tests agreeing the series is stationary, or both agreeing it is non-stationary, gives confidence in that direction; ADF saying stationary while KPSS says non-stationary suggests a difference-stationary series that needs differencing; and the reverse disagreement suggests a trend-stationary series that should be detrended, or low test power on a short or noisy sample. The procedure turns the question 'should I difference this series before modeling it' from a visual guess into a decision backed by two tests with known error rates, and it sets the differencing order d in an ARIMA(p, d, q) model. The test specification (constant only versus constant plus trend) has to match the series, or both tests can mislead.

concepts.title: Markov Chains and Hidden Markov Models
concepts.description: The Markov property says a chain's future depends on its full history only through its current state. Transition matrices and their powers give one-step and multi-step transition probabilities, stationary distributions describe where the chain settles in the long run, and Hidden Markov Models add a layer of unobserved states. HMMs are a conceptual ancestor of modern sequence models and are still used for tasks like part-of-speech tagging.
learningObjectives: State the Markov property and explain why it makes a chain's future depend only on its current state, not its full history, without implying the process has no memory at all.
Construct and use a transition probability matrix, and compute multi-step transition probabilities via matrix powers.
Define a stationary distribution of a Markov chain, compute it for a small example, and connect the concept to weak stationarity for time series.
Explain how a Hidden Markov Model extends a Markov chain by adding a hidden state layer that emits observable outputs, distinguishing transition probabilities from emission probabilities.
Describe a concrete HMM application such as part-of-speech tagging, and explain why Markov chains and HMMs are considered a conceptual ancestor of modern sequence models.

sections.heading: The Markov Property: Memorylessness in a Precise Sense
sections.body:
A discrete-time, discrete-state **Markov chain** is a sequence of random variables `X_0, X_1, X_2, ...`, each taking a value from a fixed set of states, that satisfies the **Markov property**: `P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i, X_(t-1), X_(t-2), ..., X_0) = P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i)`. In plain language, once you know the current state, knowing the *entire* history that led up to it adds nothing to your ability to predict what happens next: the future is conditionally independent of the past, given the present.

It is easy to over-interpret this as "the process has no memory at all," which is a misreading to correct up front. The Markov property is about the *transition rule*, not about how much history the current state may summarize: a state can be designed to encode as much of the relevant past as you need. A chain whose state is "the last 3 words typed" satisfies the Markov property with respect to *that* state definition, even though it depends on more than the immediately preceding instant. What is memoryless is that, given this state, nothing about *how* the process arrived there changes the transition probabilities. Choosing what the state represents is a design decision with consequences, not a limitation of the mathematics.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
states = ["Sunny", "Rainy"]
transition = {
    "Sunny": {"Sunny": 0.8, "Rainy": 0.2},
    "Rainy": {"Sunny": 0.4, "Rainy": 0.6},
}

def step(current_state):
    options = list(transition[current_state].keys())
    probs = list(transition[current_state].values())
    return rng.choice(options, p=probs)

# Two different histories (path_a, path_b) that both end in "Sunny" on day 2:
# the Markov property says what happens next does not depend on how that "Sunny" was reached.
path_a = ["Sunny", "Rainy", "Sunny"]
path_b = ["Rainy", "Rainy", "Sunny"]
print("Both paths reach 'Sunny' at day 2 via different histories.")
print("day-3 transition probabilities depend ONLY on 'Sunny':", transition["Sunny"])
```

Whichever history (`path_a` or `path_b`) led to "Sunny" on day 2, the code has no way to look at it when deciding day 3's probabilities: `transition["Sunny"]` is looked up by the current state alone. That is the Markov property in code. (`step` and `rng` are defined but only used if you extend the example to simulate; the two paths only illustrate the lookup.)

sections.heading: Transition Matrices and Multi-Step Transitions
sections.body:
A Markov chain's **transition matrix** `P` collects every one-step transition probability into a single object: `P[i, j] = P(X_(t+1) = j | X_t = i)`. Every row of `P` is a full probability distribution over "where do I go next, given I'm currently in state i," so every row must sum to 1 (a state has to go *somewhere*, including possibly staying put).

Multi-step transition probabilities follow directly from matrix multiplication, via a result called the **Chapman-Kolmogorov equation**: the probability of going from state `i` to state `j` in exactly 2 steps is `P(X_(t+2)=j | X_t=i) = sum over k of P[i,k] * P[k,j]`, summing over every intermediate state `k` the chain could have passed through. That is the definition of matrix multiplication, `(P @ P)[i, j]`. This generalizes cleanly: the `n`-step transition probabilities are given by the `n`-th matrix power, `P^n`.

```python
import numpy as np

states = ["Sunny", "Rainy"]
P = np.array([
    [0.8, 0.2],   # from Sunny: 80% Sunny, 20% Rainy
    [0.4, 0.6],   # from Rainy: 40% Sunny, 60% Rainy
])

print("rows sum to 1:", P.sum(axis=1))

P2 = P @ P                          # 2-step transition probabilities
P5 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 5)   # 5-step transition probabilities
P50 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 50)  # 50-step transition probabilities

print("P^2:\n", np.round(P2, 3))
print("P^5:\n", np.round(P5, 3))
print("P^50:\n", np.round(P50, 3))
# P^2 = [[0.72 0.28] [0.56 0.44]]   P^5 = [[0.67 0.33] [0.66 0.34]]   P^50 = [[0.667 0.333] [0.667 0.333]]
```

As the power grows, the two rows of `P^n` approach each other: by `P^5` they already agree to about 0.01 (0.67 against 0.66), and `P^50` has two identical rows, both (0.667, 0.333). After enough steps the probability of being Sunny is the same whether you started Sunny or Rainy. The chain has forgotten its starting point and converged to a single long-run distribution over states, the stationary distribution introduced in the next section.

sections.heading: Stationary Distributions: Where the Chain Settles
sections.body:
A **stationary distribution** of a Markov chain is a row vector `pi` (a probability distribution over the states, so its entries are non-negative and sum to 1) satisfying `pi @ P = pi` -- if the chain's current state distribution is `pi`, then applying one more transition step leaves the distribution unchanged. If the chain is **irreducible** (every state is reachable from every other state), this `pi` is unique. If it is also **aperiodic** (it doesn't cycle through states in a rigid fixed-length loop), the chain's distribution converges to `pi` from *any* starting distribution as the number of steps grows, as seen numerically with `P^50` in the previous section. (A chain that alternates deterministically between two states has a stationary distribution but never converges to it.)

The naming echoes the first concept in this module. A chain started in its stationary distribution is a stationary process in the sense of that concept: the distribution of the state at every time, and of any window of states, is the same whatever the starting time. "Stationary" in both places means a statistical description that the dynamics leave unchanged.

```python
import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.8, 0.2],
    [0.4, 0.6],
])

# Solve pi @ P = pi, sum(pi) = 1 via the eigenvector of P^T with eigenvalue 1.
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(P.T)
stationary_index = np.argmin(np.abs(eigenvalues - 1.0))
pi = np.real(eigenvectors[:, stationary_index])
pi = pi / pi.sum()

print("stationary distribution pi:", np.round(pi, 3))
print("check pi @ P == pi:", np.round(pi @ P, 3))

P50 = np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 50)
print("P^50 rows (should both match pi):\n", np.round(P50, 3))
# pi = [0.667 0.333]; both rows of P^50 = [0.667 0.333]
```

`pi` is `[2/3, 1/3]`: two-thirds Sunny, one-third Rainy in the long run. You can check it by hand from `pi @ P = pi`: 0.8 * pi_S + 0.4 * pi_R = pi_S gives pi_S = 2 * pi_R, and with the two summing to 1, pi = (2/3, 1/3). Both rows of `P^50` match, so the eigenvector solution and the matrix-power convergence agree. Having two independent ways to compute the same long-run answer is a good cross-check.

sections.heading: Hidden Markov Models: Adding a Layer You Can't Observe
sections.body:
A **Hidden Markov Model (HMM)** adds one more layer on top of an ordinary Markov chain: the chain's states, `Z_t`, are never directly observed -- they're **hidden** -- and at each step, the current hidden state emits an observable output `X_t` according to an **emission distribution** (often written as an emission matrix `B`, where `B[i, k] = P(X_t = k | Z_t = i)`), which is a different object from the transition matrix `A` governing how the hidden states themselves evolve. You only ever get to see the sequence of emitted outputs `X_1, X_2, ..., X_T`; the goal is almost always to infer something about the hidden sequence `Z_1, ..., Z_T` that plausibly produced it.

A concrete toy example makes the moving parts tangible: imagine hidden weather states {Rainy, Sunny} with some transition matrix `A` governing how the weather itself evolves day to day, and an emission matrix `B` describing the probability of observing someone doing {Walk, Shop, Clean} conditioned on the day's (hidden, unobserved-by-you) weather. Given only a sequence of observed activities, an HMM lets you compute both the overall likelihood of that observed sequence, and, at each time step, a probability distribution over what the hidden weather most likely was -- without ever directly seeing the weather itself.

```python
import numpy as np

states = ["Rainy", "Sunny"]
observations = ["Walk", "Shop", "Clean"]

A = np.array([        # hidden-state transition matrix
    [0.7, 0.3],        # from Rainy: 70% Rainy, 30% Sunny
    [0.4, 0.6],        # from Sunny: 40% Rainy, 60% Sunny
])
B = np.array([        # emission matrix: P(observation | hidden state)
    [0.1, 0.4, 0.5],   # Rainy  -> P(Walk), P(Shop), P(Clean)
    [0.6, 0.3, 0.1],   # Sunny  -> P(Walk), P(Shop), P(Clean)
])
pi0 = np.array([0.6, 0.4])   # initial distribution over hidden states

obs_sequence = [0, 2, 1]   # Walk, Clean, Shop  (indices into `observations`)

def forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0):
    n_states = A.shape[0]
    T = len(obs_sequence)
    alpha = np.zeros((T, n_states))
    alpha[0] = pi0 * B[:, obs_sequence[0]]
    for t in range(1, T):
        for j in range(n_states):
            alpha[t, j] = np.sum(alpha[t - 1] * A[:, j]) * B[j, obs_sequence[t]]
    likelihood = alpha[-1].sum()
    filtered = alpha / alpha.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # normalize each row to get P(hidden state | obs so far)
    return likelihood, filtered

likelihood, filtered_probs = forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0)
print("P(observed sequence 'Walk, Clean, Shop'):", round(likelihood, 5))
print("filtered hidden-state probabilities per day:\n", np.round(filtered_probs, 3))
# P(observed sequence 'Walk, Clean, Shop'): 0.03104
# filtered rows (Rainy, Sunny): [0.2 0.8], [0.81 0.19], [0.706 0.294]
```

`forward_algorithm` implements the dynamic-programming **forward algorithm**. `alpha[t, j]` is the probability of having observed everything up to time `t` *and* being in hidden state `j` at time `t`. It is built recursively from `alpha[t-1]` with the transition-matrix idea from earlier sections, then weighted by how likely state `j` is to have produced the observation at time `t`. Normalizing each row gives the *filtered* probabilities, P(hidden state | observations so far). The **Viterbi algorithm** (not implemented here) finds the single *most likely* hidden state sequence instead, using a nearly identical recursion with `max` in place of `sum` plus back-pointers to recover the path.

HMMs were the dominant technique for **part-of-speech tagging** (hidden state = grammatical tag, observed output = the actual word) and speech recognition (hidden state = phoneme, observed output = an acoustic frame) for years before neural sequence models displaced them for large-scale production use. Their core pattern, a compact hidden state updated one step at a time as new input arrives and summarizing what matters about the sequence so far, is the one an RNN's hidden state later generalized (dropping the discrete-state and strict-Markov restrictions), and attention-based models went further. Plain Markov chains and small HMMs are still used directly for lightweight sequence tasks (simple text generators, baseline POS taggers, bioinformatics sequence models) where a neural sequence model would be overkill, and working through them by hand is a good route to intuition before a full neural sequence-modeling course.

examples.title: Simulating a Random Trajectory Through the Chain
examples.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
states = ["Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy"]
P = np.array([
    [0.6, 0.3, 0.1],
    [0.3, 0.4, 0.3],
    [0.2, 0.3, 0.5],
])

def simulate_chain(P, states, start_index, n_steps):
    current = start_index
    path = [states[current]]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        current = rng.choice(len(states), p=P[current])
        path.append(states[current])
    return path

trajectory = simulate_chain(P, states, start_index=0, n_steps=15)
print(" -> ".join(trajectory))

# Empirically estimate the long-run fraction of time spent in each state from one long run.
long_run = simulate_chain(P, states, start_index=0, n_steps=20000)
from collections import Counter
counts = Counter(long_run)
total = len(long_run)
print({state: round(counts[state] / total, 3) for state in states})
# {'Sunny': 0.391, 'Cloudy': 0.332, 'Rainy': 0.276}
examples.explanation: The 15-step trajectory is one plausible path through the chain, sampled at each step from the current state's row of P with `rng.choice`, the simulation counterpart of 'multiply by P'. The empirical fractions over 20,000 steps (0.391, 0.332, 0.276) are close to the stationary distribution from the matrix power, (0.389, 0.333, 0.278). A long single trajectory's time average converges to the distribution that the matrix-power calculation reaches, a basic instance of the ergodic property of irreducible, aperiodic chains.

examples.title: Toy HMM: Inferring Likely Hidden Weather From Observed Activities
examples.code:
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.7, 0.3], [0.4, 0.6]])       # hidden transition: Rainy, Sunny
B = np.array([[0.1, 0.4, 0.5], [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]])  # emission: Walk, Shop, Clean
pi0 = np.array([0.6, 0.4])

def forward_algorithm(obs_sequence, A, B, pi0):
    T, n_states = len(obs_sequence), A.shape[0]
    alpha = np.zeros((T, n_states))
    alpha[0] = pi0 * B[:, obs_sequence[0]]
    for t in range(1, T):
        for j in range(n_states):
            alpha[t, j] = np.sum(alpha[t - 1] * A[:, j]) * B[j, obs_sequence[t]]
    return alpha

obs_walk_walk_clean = [0, 0, 2]   # Walk, Walk, Clean
obs_clean_clean_clean = [2, 2, 2]  # Clean, Clean, Clean

for name, obs in [("Walk,Walk,Clean", obs_walk_walk_clean), ("Clean,Clean,Clean", obs_clean_clean_clean)]:
    alpha = forward_algorithm(obs, A, B, pi0)
    filtered = alpha / alpha.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    print(f"{name}: P(sequence)={alpha[-1].sum():.5f}, final day P(Rainy)={filtered[-1, 0]:.3f}")
examples.explanation: Walk, Walk, Clean ends with a filtered final-day probability of 0.795 Rainy: the two Walks (emitted far more often by Sunny, 0.6 against 0.1) make the earlier days look Sunny, but the final Clean (0.5 under Rainy against 0.1 under Sunny) outweighs them, and the transition matrix carries only part of the earlier evidence forward. Clean, Clean, Clean pushes the final-day probability higher, to 0.911 Rainy. The sequence likelihoods are 0.03052 and 0.04590. In neither case does the model observe the weather; every conclusion about the hidden state comes from how consistent each possible hidden-state sequence is with the emission probabilities of what was observed, which is the inferential point of an HMM.

misconceptions.description: The Markov property means the process has no memory at all -- it can't meaningfully use any information from before the current instant.
misconceptions.clarification: The Markov property says only that the future is conditionally independent of the past GIVEN the current state; it says nothing about how much history that state may summarize. A state can encode an arbitrary amount of relevant history (for instance, 'the last k observations' instead of only the most recent one), and the chain built on that richer state still satisfies the Markov property with respect to it. 'Memoryless' describes the transition rule's dependence structure, not an absolute limit on how much of the past matters.
misconceptions.fact: The Markov property says only that the future is conditionally independent of the past given the current state; it says nothing about how much history that state may summarize.

misconceptions.description: In a Hidden Markov Model, the observed outputs are effectively the same thing as the hidden states -- 'hidden' just means the states haven't been looked at yet, and can be read straight off the observations.
misconceptions.clarification: Hidden states in an HMM cannot be read off the emitted outputs: the premise of the model is that one observation could have been emitted by several different hidden states, each with some probability under the emission distribution. Recovering information about the hidden sequence takes probabilistic inference over both the transition and emission probabilities (the forward algorithm for filtered probabilities, the Viterbi algorithm for the single most likely sequence), not a lookup.

    [0.9, 0.1],
    [0.5, 0.5],

exercises.solutionExplanation: Starting with certainty in state 0 (pi0 = [1.0, 0.0]), one step forward reads off state 0's row of P, giving pi1 = [0.9, 0.1]. The second step combines both of P's rows, weighted by how likely each state was after step 1: 90% weight on row 0 ([0.9, 0.1]) and 10% weight on row 1 ([0.5, 0.5]), giving pi2 = 0.9*[0.9, 0.1] + 0.1*[0.5, 0.5] = [0.86, 0.14]. This is the Chapman-Kolmogorov idea: summing over every intermediate state the chain could have been in at step 1. It matches `pi0 @ np.linalg.matrix_power(P, 2)`, computed one step at a time.

    [0.5, 0.3, 0.1],   # BUG: this row sums to 0.9, not 1.0
    [0.2, 0.5, 0.3],
    [0.1, 0.2, 0.7],

import numpy as np

P = np.array([
    [0.5, 0.3, 0.2],   # FIXED: now sums to 1.0
    [0.2, 0.5, 0.3],

])

def is_valid_transition_matrix(P, tol=1e-9):
    non_negative = (P >= 0).all()
    rows_sum_to_one = np.allclose(P.sum(axis=1), 1.0, atol=tol)
    return non_negative and rows_sum_to_one

print("valid:", is_valid_transition_matrix(P))

exercises.solutionExplanation: A valid transition matrix needs two conditions: every entry non-negative, and every row summing to 1, because each row is a complete probability distribution over 'where does the chain go next.' The original `is_valid_transition_matrix` only checked non-negativity, so it returned True for a matrix whose first row summed to 0.9, leaving 10% of the probability mass unaccounted for. The problem surfaced only when `rng.choice(3, p=P[0])` ran downstream, which requires `p` to sum to 1 (within a small tolerance) and raises a ValueError otherwise. The fix adds the missing row-sum check (using `np.allclose` rather than exact equality, to tolerate floating-point rounding) and corrects the broken row's third value from 0.1 to 0.2 so it genuinely sums to 1.0.

assessments.prompt: Which statement best captures the Markov property?
options: The process must have a finite number of possible states, or the Markov property does not apply.

Given the current state, the probability distribution over the next state does not depend on any additional information about the states visited before the current one -- the future is conditionally independent of the past given the present.
The process has no memory of anything before the current time step, and no amount of state engineering can change that.
Every state must have exactly the same probability of transitioning to every other state.
assessments.explanation: Conditioning on the current state makes the past irrelevant to predicting the future: the transition rule depends only on the present state, not on the trajectory that led there. The “The process has no memory of anything…” option overstates the property into 'no memory at all', the misconception this concept corrects, since the current state can summarize arbitrary history. The “Every state must have exactly the same…” option invents a uniform-transition requirement unrelated to the Markov property. The “The process must have a finite number…” option is false; the Markov property is commonly discussed for discrete-state chains but the underlying conditional-independence idea extends to continuous-state processes as well.

assessments.prompt: A stationary distribution pi of a Markov chain with transition matrix P satisfies which equation, and what does that equation mean?
options: P @ pi = 0 -- the stationary distribution is any vector that the transition matrix maps to the zero vector after one step of the chain.
sum(pi) = 0 -- the stationary distribution's entries must cancel out to zero.
pi @ P = pi -- if the chain's current state distribution is pi, applying one more transition step leaves the distribution unchanged.
pi = P^(-1) -- the stationary distribution is the matrix inverse of the transition matrix.
assessments.explanation: pi @ P = pi is the defining equation of a stationary distribution: a fixed point of the one-step transition, so the distribution over states is unchanged by another step. That is also why, under irreducibility and aperiodicity, P^n for large n converges to a matrix whose rows all equal pi. The “P @ pi = 0…” option describes an unrelated null-space condition that isn't how a stationary distribution is defined. The “pi = P^(-1) -- the stationary distribution…” option makes no sense here: pi is a probability vector, not a matrix, and P^(-1) (even where it exists) does not define stationarity. The “sum(pi) = 0 -- the stationary distribution's…” option contradicts the basic requirement that a probability distribution's entries sum to 1, not 0.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a colleague building a simple part-of-speech tagger what the Markov property buys you computationally, what 'hidden' means in a Hidden Markov Model, and why understanding these classical models is a useful step before diving into RNNs or transformer-based sequence models.
assessments.modelAnswer: The Markov property says that once you know a sequence's current state, nothing about the specific path that led to that state changes the probabilities of what happens next -- the future only depends on the past through the present state. Computationally this matters a great deal: instead of tracking and conditioning on an ever-growing history, you carry forward a single current state (or, in the forward algorithm, a small vector of probabilities over hidden states) and a fixed transition rule. That is what makes dynamic-programming algorithms like the forward and Viterbi algorithms efficient; without the Markov property, the computation would have to consider exponentially many histories instead of a compact running summary. In a Hidden Markov Model built for part-of-speech tagging, the hidden states are the true grammatical tags (noun, verb, and so on) that generated each word, and 'hidden' means those tags are never directly given to the model -- only the sequence of words themselves is observed. A single word can plausibly have been generated by more than one tag (the word 'run' could be a verb or a noun), so recovering the most likely tag sequence requires genuine probabilistic inference that weighs both how likely each tag is to emit the observed word (the emission probabilities) and how likely one tag is to follow another (the transition probabilities), rather than reading tags straight off the words. Understanding Markov chains and HMMs before moving on to RNNs or transformers is valuable because they make the hidden-state-plus-transition-rule idea explicit and small enough to compute by hand. An RNN's hidden state, and later attention over a full sequence, are much more flexible generalizations of the same pattern: keep a compact summary of everything relevant seen so far, update it one step at a time as new input arrives, and use it to explain or predict the next observation.
